name: Secure distributed multiple imputation enables missing data inference for private datasets
summary: Multiple imputation by chained equations carried out across parties that cannot share their data, implemented twice -- once over secure multiparty computation and once over multiparty homomorphic encryption -- in under 550 lines of Pythonic code. The work extends the Codon stack twice over: it is written in Sequre, itself Codon-based, and the authors added distributed data types and new compiler optimization passes to Sequre to make the MHE path compile, then reimplemented Lattigo's distributed CKKS scheme in Codon so the encryption, rotation and collective bootstrapping primitives exist there at all.
why_codon: The paper states both variants were implemented in Sequre, described there as a Codon-based Pythonic DSL, that Sequre was extended with distributed data types and compiler optimization passes, and that Lattigo's distributed CKKS scheme was reimplemented in Codon.
note: First paper-to-repository join in the index: this is the published account of 0xTCG/secure-mice, whose four .codon files the repository lane recorded as reaching Codon through Sequre. The paper confirms that reading and goes further -- the Codon layer itself was extended, which the repository alone did not show.

name: seqproc: An efficient, flexible, and concise tool for sequence geometry description
summary: A tool for describing the geometry of sequencing reads -- where barcodes, UMIs and biological sequence sit within a read -- so that pre-processing can be specified declaratively and left to a backend. Seq is discussed in the related-work section on domain-specific languages for sequence analysis, credited with extending Python with genomics primitives and compiler optimizations for sequence pipelines, and set alongside SARVAVID and BioJulia as prior systems addressing sequence processing. seqproc does not build on it.
why_codon: The full text cites Seq once, in the survey of DSLs and specialized libraries applied to sequence analysis, and runs nothing.
note: Seq is cited here as a peer of BioJulia and SARVAVID rather than as an ancestor. The bioRxiv pdf path in OpenAlex 404s; the /content/<doi>v1.full.pdf form served it.

name: Pytrf: a python package for finding tandem repeats from genomic sequences
summary: A Python package for identifying tandem repeats genome-wide, written to fill what the authors describe as a gap: no efficient tandem-repeat tool integrates cleanly with the Python ecosystem. The Nature Biotechnology Seq paper is cited in support of the claim that Python has become the common language for genomic data analysis, so it appears as evidence for the premise rather than as a technology the work uses.
why_codon: The single inline citation supports the sentence that Python has emerged as the most commonly used language for deciphering genomic data. Nothing is run.
note: A citation of the Nature Biotechnology paper as evidence about Python's popularity, not about Codon or Seq. The venue choice of that paper gives it a reach the compiler papers do not have, and this is what that reach looks like in practice.

name: Easy Acceleration with Distributed Arrays
summary: An argument for distributed arrays, in the partitioned global address space sense, as a route to both horizontal and vertical scaling without exposing threading and message passing to the user. Codon is cited once, in a list of high-level languages in which distributed arrays have been implemented effectively, beside Matlab, Octave and Python. It is a pointer to Python-family tooling rather than an engagement with the compiler.
why_codon: The full text carries one bracketed citation of the Codon reference, in the sentence listing high-level languages where distributed arrays can be implemented effectively.
note: Resolved through the arXiv copy at 2508.17493, which OpenAlex listed as a green location while the IEEE page carries no PDF.
